definition: How a portfolio is divided among stocks, bonds and cash.
A group of investments that behave similarly, such as stocks, bonds, cash or real estate.
A fall of 20 percent or more in a market from its recent high.
How much a stock tends to move compared with the overall market; 1 means in line with it.
The gap between the highest price a buyer offers (bid) and the lowest price a seller accepts (ask).
A large, well-established and financially sound company with a long record of stable earnings.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest and returns the principal at maturity.
A firm that buys and sells investments on behalf of its customers.
A sustained rise in market prices, commonly 20 percent or more from a recent low.
The profit from selling an investment for more than its cost basis.
Interest earned on both the original amount and on interest already earned.
A market fall of 10 to 20 percent from a recent high.
The original value of an investment for tax purposes, usually the purchase price plus fees.
The fixed interest payment a bond makes, stated as a percentage of its face value.
An agency's opinion of how likely a borrower is to repay its debt, from AAA down to D.
Spreading money across many investments so that no single one can cause serious damage.
A payment, usually in cash, that a company makes to shareholders out of its profits.
A stock's yearly dividend divided by its share price.
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price.
A measure, in years, of how sensitive a bond's price is to interest rate changes.
A company's profit divided by its number of shares.
How many equal-sized positions a portfolio behaves like; lower means more concentrated.
Three to six months of essential expenses kept in a safe, easily accessed account.
Exchange-traded fund: a basket of investments that trades on an exchange like a single share.
The yearly cost of owning a fund, as a percentage of the amount invested.
The amount a bond repays at maturity, also called par value or principal.
A person or firm legally required to act in a client's best interest.
A US employer-sponsored retirement plan funded by contributions from each paycheck.
A measure that tracks the performance of a group of securities, such as the S&P 500.
A fund built to match the performance of a market index at low cost.
The general rise in prices over time, which reduces what money can buy.
Individual Retirement Account: a US tax-advantaged retirement account opened by an individual.
An order to buy or sell only at a specified price or better.
How quickly and cheaply an asset can be converted to cash.
The total value of a company's shares: share price times shares outstanding.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price.
The date on which a bond's principal is repaid.
A pooled investment bought from the fund company once a day at its net asset value.
The per-share value of a fund's holdings minus its liabilities.
Share price divided by earnings per share; what investors pay for each dollar of profit.
The full collection of investments a person holds.
The original amount invested or lent, before interest or growth.
An investment's return after subtracting inflation.
Buying and selling to bring a portfolio back to its target mix.
A significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months.
Real estate investment trust: a company that owns income-producing property and trades like a stock.
Your willingness to see investments fall in value without abandoning your plan.
A US retirement account funded with after-tax money whose qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
A group of companies in the same part of the economy, such as technology or healthcare.
Return above the risk-free rate divided by volatility; return earned per unit of risk.
A share of ownership in a company.
An all-in-one fund that shifts from stocks to bonds as a chosen year approaches.
Selling an investment at a loss to offset taxable gains.
The short code that identifies a traded security, such as AAPL.
How long money will stay invested before it is needed.
Debt issued by the US government, regarded as having very low credit risk.
How much and how quickly an investment's price moves up and down.
A US rule that disallows a tax loss if the same security is bought within 30 days of the sale.
The income an investment pays, as a percentage of its price.
The total yearly return of a bond if bought today and held until it matures.
